analysis.one_liner: Bans new mining on federal land beside the Boundary Waters wilderness in Minnesota.
analysis.headline: The House committee approved the mining withdrawal 19-16 on September 30, 2020, and reported it on December 18, but the House never voted before the term ended January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would permanently withdraw about 234,328 acres of federal land and water in Minnesota's Rainy River Watershed — next to the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness and upstream of Voyageurs National Park — from all mining claim staking, mineral leasing, and disposal. The Forest Service could still allow removal of sand, gravel, granite, iron ore, and taconite if it found that doing so would not harm the watershed's water, air, or forest habitat. It passed out of committee on a narrow 19-16 vote but never received a House floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who canoe, fish, and hunt in and around the Boundary Waters, the outfitters and tourism businesses that depend on an unspoiled wilderness, and residents who rely on the clean water of the Rainy River Watershed, which flows through Voyageurs National Park. Sulfide-ore copper mining in this watershed carries a well-known risk of acid mine drainage that can contaminate water for decades, so blocking new mineral entry protects the water that recreation and the local tourism economy depend on.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Paddlers, anglers, and Minnesota tourism businesses

how_it_helps.text: Permanently bars new mining claims, mineral leasing, and disposal on roughly 234,328 acres of Superior National Forest in the Rainy River Watershed, the area draining into the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness and Voyageurs National Park.
Extends the withdrawal to any land the United States acquires in the area after enactment, so the protection grows rather than shrinks.

Keeps traditional northern Minnesota mineral uses alive by letting the Forest Service approve removal of sand, gravel, granite, iron ore, and taconite whenever it determines the removal would not damage the watershed's water quality, air quality, or forest habitat.

analysis.who_pays: Companies holding or seeking federal mineral rights in the watershed lose the ability to develop them — chiefly sulfide-ore copper-nickel miners, whose standard method can generate acid drainage that pollutes water long after a mine closes. Northeastern Minnesota communities that were counting on copper-nickel mine jobs and tax revenue would forgo that development. Taconite, iron ore, and aggregate operators keep a path forward, but only with Forest Service approval.
analysis.who_pays_short: Copper-nickel mining companies and mineral-rights holders

drawbacks.text: The withdrawal forecloses mineral development and the jobs and tax base it could have brought to northeastern Minnesota's mining region, a real cost that area officials have long cited in opposing Boundary Waters mining bans.

The bill covers only about 234,328 federal acres and honors valid existing rights, so mining can still occur on nearby state, private, and already-claimed lands in the same watershed — pollution does not respect the withdrawal boundary.

The protection is not absolute: the Forest Service may still permit removal of iron ore, taconite, granite, and sand, so the strength of the safeguard depends on the judgment of whichever administration runs the Forest Service.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is clean water and a nationally significant wilderness versus forgone copper-nickel development in a region that wants mining jobs. The bill tried to soften that tradeoff — it exempts taconite and iron ore, the region's traditional industry, unless they would harm the watershed — and it protects only federal land, leaving state and private development options open. The cost is real but narrow and local; the benefit, permanent protection of a watershed that cannot be un-polluted, is broad and irreversible. On balance the benefits outweigh the costs, though an honest supporter should acknowledge the bill would not fully shield the watershed from mining on nearby non-federal land.

outcome.mechanism: The committee approved it in September 2020 and formally reported it on December 18, 2020, but with the Congress ending on January 3, 2021, the House never brought it up for a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced January 14, 2020 by Rep. Betty McCollum with original cosponsors including Republicans Francis Rooney and Fred Upton, and was referred to the Natural Resources Committee and two of its subcommittees.
A subcommittee hearing was held February 5, 2020, and on September 30, 2020 the subcommittees were discharged and the full committee approved the bill as amended on a narrow 19-16 vote.

On December 18, 2020 — about two weeks before the Congress expired — the committee reported the amended bill as H. Rept. 116-672 and it was placed on the Union Calendar, where House bills wait to be scheduled for a floor vote.
No House floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Copper-nickel mining interests came out ahead: because the bill never became law, the federal minerals in the Rainy River Watershed remain open to claim-staking and leasing, leaving the door open for projects like Twin Metals' proposed mine. Businesses and visitors who wanted the watershed permanently shielded from mining got nothing.

for.name: Betty McCollum
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and assembled 48 cosponsors; its Minnesota sponsor.

for.name: Raúl Grijalva
for.what_they_did: Discharged the bill from subcommittees, held the markup, and moved it through committee to a formal House report.

for.name: 3 of 197 House Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors, including original cosponsors Francis Rooney and Fred Upton

against.name: Natural Resources Committee Republicans (16 members)
against.what_they_did: Voted against reporting the bill out of committee, which passed 19-16.

against.name: Twin Metals Minnesota
against.role: Copper-nickel mining company (owned by Chilean mining group Antofagasta)
against.what_they_did: Opposed the withdrawal of the federal lands its proposed mine would depend on.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor after it was placed on the Union Calendar on December 18, 2020; the term ended without a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 45 of 231 House Democrats versus 3 of 197 House Republicans cosponsored — and the committee vote was narrow at 19-16, though a handful of Republicans backed the bill from the start.

industries.note: The bill would bar new claims and leases across the watershed, blocking projects like Twin Metals' proposed mine beside the Boundary Waters. Sulfide-ore mining risks acid drainage that can contaminate water for decades, so the industry's interest here runs directly against the water quality that residents and the recreation economy depend on.

industries.industry: Taconite, iron ore, and aggregate producers
industries.note: The bill does not ban them: the Forest Service may still approve removal of iron ore, taconite, granite, and sand, conditioned on a finding that it would not harm the watershed. Traditional Iron Range operations keep a legal path forward, though with a new federal review layer.

Outfitters, guides, and lodging businesses in northeastern Minnesota earn their living from visitors drawn to an unspoiled Boundary Waters, and permanent protection of the watershed safeguards the resource they depend on.
